column1: # player-vocabulary.tsv — THE banned-jargon list, in ONE place, read by TWO checkers.
# ⚑ WHY IT IS A FILE AND NOT A RUST CONST. It began as `PRIVATE_VOCABULARY` inside
#   `dreggnet-web/src/guide.rs`'s test module, where it gated exactly ONE function
#   (`guide_body()`). `/guide` scored 0 violations while an audit found the same list broken on
#   6 of 13 live surfaces — the gate was not wrong, its SCOPE was one function wide. Widening it
#   meant a second reader (`scripts/check-player-vocabulary.py`, which sweeps every page), and a
#   second reader must never mean a second list: two lists drift, and the day they drift the
#   weaker one is the one that decides. So the list moved HERE and both readers parse it:
#     * `scripts/check-player-vocabulary.py`   — every player-facing web surface, from source.
#     * `dreggnet-web/src/guide.rs`'s tests    — `include_str!` on this file, over the RENDERED
#                                                `/guide` body (which catches jargon composed in
#                                                from another module, as source-reading cannot).
# ⚑ WHERE THE LIST CAME FROM. `docs/reference/UX-QA-SWEEP-2026-07-26.md`: four first-time readers
#   were handed the rendered pages. One could not produce a one-sentence answer to "what is this
#   site" because *"the sentence describing what the site IS is itself written in the site's
#   private vocabulary"*. Their verdict on the sixteen flagged terms: *"not a nitpick list; it's
#   the majority of the page's distinctive vocabulary."*
# ⚑ THIS IS NOT A SPELLING RULE. A banned term needs a replacement that is TRUE, not vaguer.
#   Swapping a precise word for a fuzzy one is the same error as the overclaim it replaced, only
#   quieter. The third column is the replacement STRATEGY, not a substitution table: `receipt`
#   does not become one word, it becomes whatever that page's record actually does for a reader.
#   Where a term is genuinely load-bearing and has no plain equivalent, it stays and takes a row
#   in `scripts/player-vocabulary-allow.tsv` with the reason.
# Three TAB-separated fields:
#     term <TAB> why a newcomer cannot read it <TAB> what to say instead
# Matching is SUBSTRING, case-insensitive, so `receipt` also catches `receipts` and `Receipt`.
# Deliberately NOT here: `crowned`, `guild`/`lane`, and the straight-line move rule. Those are
# load-bearing, so they are permitted WITH a definition in place, which
# `guide.rs::the_load_bearing_terms_are_defined_in_place` checks separately.
executor
column2: the name of an internal component. A player pressed a button; they did not address a component.
column3: say what it DOES: the game re-runs the move against the rules, and refuses it if it is not allowed.

column1: substrate
column2: names the layer under the game. Nothing a player can see, press or be affected by.
column3: name the thing that actually happened, or drop the clause.

column1: refereed
column2: borrowed from the project's own writing about itself; a reader guesses at a human referee.
column3: checked against the rules, or say who checked and when.

column1: no-cheat
column2: a compound coined here. It reads as a promise without saying what stops a cheat.
column3: state the mechanism: a run gets on this board by being played again.

column1: receipt
column2: the record a landed move leaves. A newcomer reads a shop receipt and expects a total.
column3: say what the record DOES for them: it is the move, kept, so anyone can re-run it.

column1: commitment
column2: cryptographic sense, not the ordinary one. The ordinary reading is nearly opposite.
column3: a sealed value, or name what it hides and from whom.

column1: poseidon
column2: a hash function's name. Zero player meaning, and it reads as a proper noun.
column3: drop it. A player never chooses a hash.

column1: merkle
column2: a data structure's name, used as an adjective a reader cannot unpack.
column3: say what it PROVES to them, or drop the clause if it proves them nothing.

column1: journal-root
column2: an internal name for one field of the record.
column3: everything that run recorded, or name the fact being reproduced.

column1: asserted actor
column2: two private words at once. `asserted` is the honest grade; `actor` is the plumbing.
column3: the name you are playing under, taken at face value.

column1: in-process re-execution
column2: describes where the check runs, in words about the server's own architecture.

column1: testnet
column2: implies a mainnet, which does not exist. Nothing here is on a chain.
column3: drop it, or name the actual deployment.

column1: rook line
column2: a chess analogy standing IN PLACE OF the rule. A non-chess-player is simply lost.
column3: spell the rule out ("straight lines only, along a row or a column"), then offer the analogy.

column1: fog
column2: the internal name for per-viewer hiding. A player sees a card face-down, not weather.
column3: hidden from your opponent, and name who it is NOT hidden from.

column2: an unglossed glyph used as a currency. It has no name a reader can say out loud.
column3: name the currency, or use its word.
